1:
The chapter opens Job's reply to the third speech of Eliphaz, and the witnesses set the whole answer in view before weighing its first words. The reformed John Gill observes that, though Job does not so much as name his friends or direct his discourse to them, he desires nothing better than to have his cause laid before God himself, by whom he has no doubt he would be acquitted; and, against their whole theology, he means to show in this chapter that a righteous man may be afflicted of God according to his unchangeable decrees, as in the next he will show that wicked men greatly prosper — a sufficient answer, Gill thinks, to Eliphaz, after which the friends fall nearly silent. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the reply the same way: Job answers the insinuations of Eliphaz with an earnest longing after God and the assertion of his own innocence, while in the chapter that follows he will lament that his own case is but one of many, and that multitudes suffer the oppression of man unavenged as he suffers the stroke of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry catches the temper of the man who now speaks. Job is confident that his friends have done him wrong, and therefore, ill as he is, he will not give up the cause nor let them have the last word; he justifies his own resentment of his trouble, appeals from the censures of his friends to the just judgment of God, and comforts himself with the hope that God will deal favourably with him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the movement of the speech in advance: Job apologizes for his complaining, wishes to plead his cause in the presence of his Maker, from whom he knows he would receive justice, but regrets that he cannot find him; then gives himself and his cause up to God with the conviction of his own innocence and of God's justice and goodness; and yet is afraid when he considers the majesty of his Maker.

The voices do not divide. They agree that the verse is a hinge: Job turns from the men who came to instruct him and sets his face toward the God who alone can try his cause, so that all that follows — the search after God's seat, the ordering of the cause, the confidence of coming forth as gold, and the dread that closes the chapter — flows from this settled resolve to carry his appeal past his accusers to the Judge of all the earth.
2:
Job's first words are a defence of his own complaining, and the witnesses divide at once over a single Hebrew word. The reformed John Gill takes the plain sense of the Authorized Version: even to this day, after all the pretended comfort of his friends, Job's complaint is bitter — not a charge of injustice against God for afflicting him, but a lament over the greatness of afflictions too heavy for his strength, and over a God who hides his face and will not show him wherefore he contends; the things he complains of are bitter as the waters of Marah, and uttered in the bitterness of his soul. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the second line with him: the stroke, the hand of God upon him, is heavier than his groaning, so that he does not complain more than there is cause.

But the grammatical-historical witnesses hear another word beneath the "bitter." Keil and Delitzsch note that מרי usually signifies obstinacy or rebellion, and render the line "even to-day my complaint still biddeth defiance, my hand lieth heavy upon my groaning"; they weigh the Septuagint's variant, which read the consonants as "from his hand," and confess the difficulty of joining the two halves of the verse without some such expletive as "although." Charles Ellicott gives both possibilities in one breath — "still is my complaint bitter, or accounted rebellion" — and draws out the clause that all can agree on: "yet is my stroke heavier than my groaning," that is, my complaint is no just measure of my suffering.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the rebellion-reading hardest. Job, he says, has derived neither conviction nor consolation from the discourses of his friends; he grants his complaint is bitter, yet insists the affliction he endures is heavier than his complaints are loud. And Clarke adopts Mr. Good's rendering as a question flung back at the friends — "And still is my complaint rebellion?" — for from the beginning they had construed his innocent laments over unparalleled suffering as rebellion against God; the original will bear it, since מרי may be derived from מרה, "he rebelled." So the witnesses circle a real ambiguity: whether Job says his complaint is bitter, or asks whether they will still call it mutiny. On the weight of the verse they are one — the blow is greater than the groan, and Job's outcry falls short of, rather than exceeds, the misery that wrings it from him.
3:
"Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat!" — the cry lifts Job past his friends toward the God he cannot locate, and the witnesses hear in it both a legal longing and a spiritual one. The reformed John Gill supplies the unnamed object, God, a relative without an antecedent; and with Jarchi he reads "his seat" as the seat of a Judge, for Job desired to find God sitting on his throne and doing right, that justice might be done him. Yet Job may be under the hidings of God's face, Gill adds, and so at a loss where to find him; the saints know that God is everywhere, fills heaven and earth, is in his church and among his people and to be found in Christ, and yet in such a case they know not, as Mr. Broughton renders it, "how" to find him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the breathing of a soul that feels it has by sin lost God, and is undone for ever if it recover not his favour: "O that I knew how I might recover his favour, how I might come into his covenant and communion with him!" It is the cry of a poor deserted soul — "Saw you him whom my soul loveth?" — that God who has laid open the way to himself would direct it in and lead it. But Henry will not let Job off wholly, for he seems to complain too boldly, as if, could he but find the seat, he would go and demand justice of his Judge.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse and the next as one forensic wish: "Who will give me the knowledge of God, that I may find him out? I would come to his establishment" — the place or way where he has promised to communicate himself — "I would exhibit, in detail, my judgment," the cause he wishes tried, "before his face, and my mouth would I fill with convincing arguments," drawn from God's own common way of saving sinners. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott catches the pathos in fewest words: it is the piteous complaint of a man who feels that God is with him for chastisement, but not for healing. The witnesses do not divide. Whether the seat Job seeks is a mercy-seat or a judgment-seat, they agree that his longing is the longing of a clear conscience, sure that if he could but come at God he would be dealt with more justly, and more tenderly, than his friends have dealt with him.
4:
Having wished he could find God's seat, Job pictures what he would do on reaching it — "I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments." The reformed John Gill allows the words a double setting. They may be the language of a praying man, who directs his prayer to God and sets it in order before him; or they may be the language of a defendant, pleading not the justification of his person before God by works, for by these no flesh can be justified, but the justification of his cause, clearing himself of the aspersions his friends have cast, as Samuel once vindicated himself before Israel, and appealing to God to stir up himself and do him right against those who strive with him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the forensic image in their rendering — "I would lay the cause before Him, and fill my mouth with arguments" — reading the whole strophe as the speech of a man confident of his ground, who longs not to escape the trial but to open it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the courtroom picture into a lesson on prayer, in which the believer has boldness to enter the holiest and come even to the footstool of the throne of grace. We have, he says, not only liberty of access but liberty of speech: leave to be particular, ordering our cause before God, laying all our grievances before him in what method we think proper, with a freedom we durst not use with earthly princes; and leave to be importunate, not only to ask but to argue, nay, to fill our mouths with arguments — not to move God, who perfectly knows the merits of the cause, but to move ourselves, to excite our own fervency and encourage our faith.

The witnesses do not divide over the sense, only over the register. Gill hears a man arranging his defence and his appeal together; Henry hears in the same words the pattern of holy, argumentative prayer; Keil and Delitzsch hear the confident brief of one sure he will maintain the right. All agree that Job is no longer merely bewailing his lot but drawing up a case, and that the "arguments" with which he would fill his mouth are not weapons against God but pleas laid humbly before him, in the settled expectation of a candid hearing. What his friends had denied him — a fair and deliberate weighing of his cause — he is sure the Almighty would grant, and it is this certainty of an equal hearing above that makes the very thought of God's seat, dreadful as it is, a thing he can long for rather than dread.
5:
The ordering of the cause looks for a reply, and Job says he would gladly hear it: "I would know the words which he would answer me, and understand what he would say unto me." The reformed John Gill reads it of a God who hears and answers prayer in his own time and way; then, at last, Job should know the reason the Lord contended with him, and what were the sins and transgressions that had drawn down his affliction — the very thing he has all along desired to be told. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley makes the wish a submissive one: if God should discover to him any secret sins for which he contends with him, Job would humble himself before him and accept the punishment of his iniquity.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes his confidence on the character of the Judge: God would speak nothing but what was true, decree nothing that was not righteous, nor utter anything that Job could not comprehend — so that whatever the answer, it would be just, and intelligible, and worth the hearing. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet to the same end — "I should like to know the words He would answer me, and attend to what He would say to me" — the language of a man who wants not the last word for himself but the decisive word from God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the contrast that gives the verse its edge. Job knew well enough what his friends would answer him: they would condemn him and run him down. "But," says Henry in his person, "I would fain know what God would answer me, for I am sure his judgment is according to truth, which theirs is not. I cannot understand them; they talk so little to the purpose. But what he says I should understand, and therefore be fully satisfied in." This, Henry adds, becomes us in all controversies: let the word of God determine them, let us know what he answers and understand what he says. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job's craving is not for acquittal on any terms but for the truth, spoken by the only mouth whose verdict is according to it; and that a man who so longs to hear God's own answer, even if that answer should be a rebuke, is no hypocrite fleeing the light but a sufferer who trusts the Judge more than the witnesses who have condemned him.
6:
Job answers his own fear before it can master him: would God overwhelm him with sheer omnipotence? "Will he plead against me with his great power? No; but he would put strength in me." The reformed John Gill reads the confidence as covenant confidence: God does not plead against his people at all, but for them; he will not use his great strength to run them down and crush them, nor deal with them according to the strict rigour of his justice, nor stir up all his wrath, for then the spirits would fail before him and the souls he has made; whatever he does with the vessels of wrath, he will never so deal with the vessels of mercy. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears the same tenderness: God would not exhibit his majesty to strike Job dumb, but would put strength in him, treat him with tenderness, rectify his mistakes, show him what was in his favour, and temper the rigid demands of justice by the mild interpretations of equity, so that where law could not clear him, mercy would conduct all to the most favourable issue.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states it plainly — God would not use his power against Job but for him, enabling him to plead his cause and giving sentence according to the clemency he uses toward his children — and the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reaches the same reading through the grammar: "Would he contend with me in the greatness of his power? Nay; but he would have regard unto me, he would consider my case." Ellicott points back to Eliphaz, who had bidden Job acquaint himself with God and return unto him; Job answers that there is nothing he longs for more than to come into God's presence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the doctrine out. It is of great use, in everything wherein we have to do with God, to keep up good thoughts of him; and Job believes God would not deal with him by absolute sovereignty or in strict justice, not with a high hand nor a strong hand. Against those obstinate in unbelief God will plead with his great power, and their destruction will come from the glory of that power; but with his own, who love him and trust him, he deals in tender compassion, and the same strength that is engaged against proud sinners is engaged for humble saints, who prevail with him by strength derived from himself, as Jacob did. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's hope rests not on his own innocence alone but on the character of the God he seeks, who meets the humble not as a crushing adversary but as one who lends the very strength by which they plead.
7:
From the hope that God will strengthen rather than crush him, Job draws his boldest inference: "There the righteous might dispute with him; so should I be delivered for ever from my judge." The reformed John Gill takes "there" of God's seat, whether the mercy-seat where even sinners are invited to reason with God for pardon, or the judgment-seat; and by "the righteous" Job means himself, conscious of his own sincerity and, relying on it, not afraid to appear before God and reason his case — the very question in dispute with his friends being whether he was a hypocrite or a sincere and upright man.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the little word שׁם, which may be local, "there," or temporal, "then"; they decide for the temporal, so that the sense is, then, if God would but attend to him, an upright man would be contending with him — it would be satisfactorily proved that an upright man may plead with God — and they take the following verb as intensive, "I should for ever be delivered." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns that "to dispute with God sounds very harsh," and reports Mr. Good's bolder turn, "and triumphantly should I escape from my condemnation"; for the word rendered "for ever" may as well be rendered "to victory," as the Vulgate took it — "he would lead on my cause to victory." Nothing less, Clarke says, than the fullest conviction of his own innocence could have led Job to speak thus to the Judge of quick and dead.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the verse rise to a Gospel height: Job has learnt the marvellous truth that it is God the Saviour who is himself the refuge from God the Judge, and, in the solemn conviction of God's presence, he is assured that though God hide himself and seem not to interfere in his cause, yet all things work together for good to them that love him, as Rom. 8:28 has it, and that when his trial is over he will come forth like gold. Only the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley enters a caution: "there," at the throne of grace, God lays aside his majesty and judges according to his wonted clemency, and the righteous may be delivered from his damnatory sentence — yet this and some such expressions of Job, Wesley judges, cannot be excused from irreverence toward God, for which God afterwards reproves him, and Job abhors himself. So the witnesses meet and part: all read a man sure of acquittal if only he could be heard, but Wesley alone hears an over-boldness in the wish that the Lord will later rebuke, where the others hear the holy confidence of a clear conscience.
8:
The search after God's seat turns now to its anguish, the fruitless ranging of a man who cannot come at him: "Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him." The reformed John Gill hears Job returning to his cry of v.3 and now relating the several ways he took to find God and could not; he reports Cocceius's ingenious turn, that "forward" and "backward" are times to come and times past — Job looking into the future days of the Messiah, his living Redeemer, and back to the first promise made to Adam, and yet unable from either to learn why good men are afflicted — though Gill offers it only as one man's fancy.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says these two verses paint in vivid colours the distress of a soul in search of the favour of God: no means left untried, no place unexplored, a true description of the conduct of a genuine penitent. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep close to the Hebrew, noting that what is "with" a man in the inward sense is what he thinks and knows and wills, and so preparing the turn at v.10, where God's inward knowledge of Job answers Job's failure to find God. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley guards the theology: God is "not there" only as a Judge to hear and determine Job's cause, for otherwise Job well knew God to be essentially present in all places.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the complaint into three losses. Job cannot fix his thoughts, his mind so hurried by trouble that, like a man in a fright, he runs this way and that and brings nothing to a head, unable to fasten on what he knew to be in God and would have found a support. He cannot find out the cause of his troubles, having viewed his whole conversation and turned it to every side without perceiving wherein he had sinned more than others. And he cannot foresee the end, not knowing whether or when God would deliver him, seeing no sign of it, as the church once complained that there was none to tell how long. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's darkness is not unbelief in God's presence but the bewilderment of a sufferer who believes God is everywhere and yet cannot, in his extremity, lay hold of him for comfort.
9:
The search sweeps on to the remaining quarters, and the witnesses take the verse chiefly as a study of Hebrew geography. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke shows that Job here names the four cardinal points by the posture of a man who faces the sunrise: the east is qedem, "before"; the west achor, "after" or the back part; the north semol, "the left"; and the south yamin, "the right" — the same orientation found where Abraham and Lot divide the land, and shared, Clarke notes, by Hebrews, Idumeans, and Arabs alike. He finds a fine local touch in the last clause, "he hideth himself on the right hand," the south, "that I cannot see him" — for the southern sky is scarcely visible in Idumea, where Job dwelt, which is why, when Job elsewhere speaks of the southern constellations, he calls them the hidden chambers of the south in ch. 9:9.

The reformed John Gill takes "the left hand, where he doth work" of the northern part of the world, where God is said to have his seat and to have stretched out the north over the empty place; God works everywhere, he grants, but in some regions more eminently than in others, and the north has been the more peopled and active — yet what precisely Job meant by God's "work" in the north, Gill honestly confesses, is not easy to say. The witnesses do not press the point past the plain sense: that whichever way Job looks, forward or back, on the left where God works or the right where he hides himself, he cannot behold him.

Beneath the geography the verse carries the ache of the whole passage. Job is not denying that God is present in every quarter; he is confessing that the God who fills all the points of the compass will not, to his darkened sense, be found at any of them. Clarke's careful mapping and Gill's cautious guess about the north serve the same end: to show a man ranging over the whole horizon of the world and of his own thought, and meeting everywhere the same silence. The very fulness of the search — east and west, north and south, the place of God's working and the place of his hiding — measures the depth of Job's perplexity, and prepares the sudden turn of the next verse, where the seeker who cannot find gives way to the sufferer who is himself perfectly known.
10:
"But he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold" — the great turn of the chapter, where the seeker who cannot find God rests in the God who perfectly knows him. The reformed John Gill hears Job comforting himself: though he cannot find God nor trace his way, God knows where Job is and what way he takes — either the way he has taken for acceptance, his living Redeemer looked to by faith, or, more likely, the whole course of his conversation, his walk in the commandments and ordinances of the Lord; and God knows it not barely as he knows all men's ways by omniscience, but by way of approbation, approving and being well pleased with it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the metaphor with a refiner's eye: God approves Job's conduct and tries him, but like true gold Job will lose nothing in the fire; genuine gold neither alters nor diminishes in the flame, but comes out gold — and so Job went into the furnace of affliction an innocent man and will come out the same, his character losing nothing of its value or its lustre.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds here the resting-place of the whole labyrinth. After Job has all but lost himself in the maze of the divine counsels, he sits down contentedly with this thought: "Though I know not the way that he takes" — for his way is in the sea and his path in the great waters — "yet he knows the way that I take." God is acquainted with it, as the friends who judged what they did not know were not; and God approves it, accepting the way of the righteous. From this Job infers the comfort of three things: that he is but tried, the affliction meant not for his hurt but for his honour, the trial of his faith; that when sufficiently tried he shall come forth, and not be left to consume in the furnace as reprobate silver, for the trial will have an end and God will not contend for ever; and that he shall come forth as gold, pure in itself and precious to the refiner, found to be good and made to be better. Those that go gold into the furnace, Henry says, will come out no worse. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's confidence rests not on his power to find God but on God's knowledge of him, and that the very fire he cannot understand is the assayer's fire, from which a tried integrity emerges brighter than it went in.
11:
His confidence of coming forth as gold rests on a cleared conscience, and Job now sets out the evidence of it: "My foot hath held his steps, his way have I kept, and not declined." The reformed John Gill reads it of a close and constant imitation: Job had trodden in the very steps God walked in, following him in acts of holiness and righteousness, of mercy and kindness, and had not only set his foot in those steps but persisted in them, following on to imitate God and to walk worthy of him. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses "his steps" as the steps or paths God has appointed men to walk in — the way marked out, not one of Job's own devising.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the claim two edges: "I have carefully marked his providential dealings, and in his way — his pure and undefiled religion — have I walked"; Job was not only generally but particularly religious, attending to the weightier matters and not forgetting the slightest injunction. Clarke lingers, as he loves to, over an old word in Coverdale's version, "his hye strete have I holden," the "high street" being the raised and paved highway, the Latin via strata, a road built up with stones — a homely image of the beaten, public way of God's commandments, kept and not forsaken.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in "held" and "kept" the language of a hard-won perseverance. Job's foot held God's steps, that is, held fast to them, adhered closely; he endeavoured to conform himself to God's example, for good people are followers of God, and to accommodate himself to God's providence, following it step by step. His holding and keeping intimate that the tempter had used all his arts, by fraud and by force, to draw him aside; but with care and resolution, and by the grace of God, he had hitherto persevered — and those that will persevere must, like him, hold with resolution and keep with watchfulness. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job is not boasting of a sinless life but pleading a settled course, a walk in the appointed way that he had neither abandoned by apostasy nor broken by wilful transgression; and that this steady tread in God's own steps is the ground on which he dares to believe that, tried as he is, he will come forth approved.
12:
The proof of obedience rises from deed to word: "Neither have I gone back from the commandment of his lips; I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food." The reformed John Gill takes the "commandment of his lips" broadly, for Job lived before the law of Sinai, or at least without knowledge of it; some think of the seven precepts given to the sons of Noah, but Gill lets it mean any and every command God had given to Noah or Abraham or the patriarchs before Job's day, which Job kept closely and made the rule of his walk. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a man who governed himself by that commandment and would not go back from it whatever difficulties the way might hold; and he presses the striking comparison of the second line — Job esteemed the words of God's mouth more than his necessary food, could as well have lived without his daily bread, and "laid it up," as the word is, as men lay up provision against a siege. The word of God, Henry says, is to our souls what food is to our bodies, sustaining the spiritual life; and Job did as Eliphaz had urged in ch. 22:22, laying up God's words in his heart.

But the closing phrase is a knot the wesleyan-arminian and grammatical-historical witnesses work at differently. Adam Clarke prefers Mr. Good's rendering, "in my bosom have I stored up the words of his mouth," for the Asiatics carry what is precious in the bosom, and the words of God were to Job a most precious treasure. Charles Ellicott notes that the Septuagint and the Vulgate likewise read "in my bosom," but offers a second possibility from the Hebrew: "I have treasured up the words of his mouth according to the statute prescribed to me," or "from my own law" — that is, Job made it a fixed principle with himself to hoard the words of God — and he draws the phrase "more than my necessary food" alongside the Lord's word about meat that the world knows not of in John 4:32-34.

So a genuine difference of reading runs under the verse, turning on the word chukki: whether Job prized God's words above his appointed food, as the Authorized Version and Gill and Henry take it; or stored them in his bosom, with Good, the Septuagint, and the Vulgate; or treasured them as his appointed rule, as Ellicott allows. The witnesses do not divide over the substance — that Job held the word of God dearer than daily bread and never went back from it — but the same Hebrew word will return in the next verse, where its ambiguity again shapes the sense.
13:
"But he is in one mind, and who can turn him? and what his soul desireth, even that he doeth" — Job's plea of obedience breaks off against the sheer, immovable will of God, and the witnesses divide over what the terse Hebrew affirms of him. The reformed John Gill offers two references for "in one mind." It may respect God's commandments — every precept stands in full force, he never alters the thing gone out of his lips, and so Job thought it his duty to abide by them; or, more likely, it may respect God's dealings with Job, which he continues notwithstanding Job's innocence, because he is sovereign and does whatever he pleases, unchangeable in his purposes, not to be wrought upon to alter his fixed course, and never changing his mind on any account whatever.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears Job laying down good truths, whatever bad use he will presently make of them. God's counsels are immutable: "he is in one mind, and who can turn him?" — he is one with himself, has no counsellors to prevail on him to alter his purpose, and never alters his measures; prayer has prevailed to change God's way and his providence, but never his will or purpose, for known unto God are all his works. And his power is irresistible: "what his soul desires, even that he does," for men may desire many things they cannot do, but God has an incontestable sovereignty and an uncontrollable power, and none can stay his hand.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, however, reads the Hebrew otherwise. The original, he says, is literally "but he is in one," which the Vulgate renders "he alone is," and Coverdale "it is he himself alone": God has no partner; his designs are his own, formed in his infinite wisdom, and none can turn his determinations aside, so that it is vain for man to contend with his Maker. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott holds the two readings open, judging that Job here either declares God's unique sovereignty — that he is one, alone — or his unchangeableness, that he is of one mind. So the debate is real and grammatical: does the line confess a God who cannot be turned because his purpose is fixed, with Gill and Henry, or a God who cannot be withstood because he is alone and without rival, with Clarke and the Vulgate? Ellicott lets both stand, and the witnesses agree at least in this, that the verse names a will against which no creature can prevail — a truth Job holds as orthodox even as it deepens his dread.
14:
The immovable will bends now upon Job in particular: "For he performeth the thing that is appointed for me, and many such things are with him." The reformed John Gill notices that the word for "the thing appointed" is the same that closed v.12, where it was rendered "my necessary food"; some accordingly render it here "he performeth my necessary things," the things needful for me, as the Targum and Mr. Broughton take it, so that even the ambiguity of the earlier verse follows into this one. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same word as a portion or lot: "he hath appointed me my lot, and like these there are multitudes with him"; God diversifies human affairs, so that scarcely any two men have the same lot, nor the same man the same portion at all times, for God has multitudes of resources and expedients by which he governs the world. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley glosses it simply — God "performeth" the calamities he has allotted to Job, and there are "many such" examples of his proceeding with men.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the whole, "he will accomplish my appointed lot, he will complete that which he has decreed for me, and like these things there are many more with him," pointing to the like word in ch. 10:13; and he catches the strange courage in it, that Job is disposed to take the full measure of the worst, that being steeled against it he may be prepared, and, so steeled, still trusts God — a temper Ellicott ties back to the great confession of ch. 13:15.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the appointment its comfort. Whatever happens to us, it is God that performs it, and he performs all that, and only that, which was appointed, in the appointed time and method — which may silence us, since what is appointed cannot be altered, and may satisfy us too, since the God who appointed us to eternal life and glory as our end appointed this affliction as part of our way. And the "many such things" mean that our case is not singular: God does many things in providence we cannot account for, and the same afflictions are accomplished in our brethren, as 1 Pet. 5:9 reminds the suffering church. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job bows to a lot decreed and unalterable, and yet — whether they call it his portion, his necessary things, or his appointed doom — that he bows to it still trusting the hand that deals it.
15:
"Therefore am I troubled at his presence: when I consider, I am afraid of him" — the settled thought of God's unchangeable will turns, in Job, not to peace but to dread. The reformed John Gill is careful which presence troubles him: not the gracious presence Job has been seeking, but God's appearance as an enemy, laying and continuing his afflicting hand, and his appearance as a Judge come to try the cause; for though Job had earnestly desired that trial, when he thinks of God's sovereignty, the immutability of his counsels, and his perfect knowledge of all things, and does not himself know what God may have to bring against him, he might well be troubled and shrink back when it came to the point. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke hears a man who sees no end to his sufferings: God has not yet exhausted his means of trial, and it is when Job considers this that he is afraid of him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws the paradox to its finest point. Invisible though God's presence is, and undiscoverable as he was on every hand in vv.8-9, Job is caught in a strait betwixt two: afraid of God, yet longing to see him; conscious of his presence, yet unable to find him; assured of his absolute justice, and yet convinced of his own suffering innocence. His history, Ellicott says, was to the old world what the Gospel is to the new — the exhibition of a perfectly righteous man made perfect through suffering, an effort at the very problem of reconciling the inequality of life with the justice of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks how bad a use Job makes of good truths. Had he duly considered God's immutable counsel and irresistible power, he might have said, "Therefore am I easy and well reconciled to my God's way with me"; instead he says, "Therefore am I troubled at his presence." Those are of troubled spirits indeed who are troubled at the presence of God, as the psalmist who remembered God and was troubled; and Henry notes that Job here contradicts himself, for just now he was troubled at God's absence, unable to find him, and now he is troubled at his presence. There is that in God, Henry grants, which, considered apart from a Redeemer, gives cause to fear; but the witnesses agree that Job's dread here outruns his faith, and that the same knowledge of God which should have steadied him has, in his darkened frame, become a terror — the honest, unresolved fear of a saint who trusts the God he cannot yet bear to meet.
16:
Job traces his terror to its author, and does not spare the confession: it is God himself who has unmanned him. The reformed John Gill is careful that the "soft" heart here is not the tender, contrite heart of the penitent, the heart of flesh God gives in place of the heart of stone — though Job had such a heart, and God had made it so — but a weak, feeble, fearful heart, pressed and broken under affliction, unable to endure and bear up under the mighty hand of God, become as water and melting like wax within him, ready to faint and sink and die away. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it to the same effect: God has prostrated Job's strength and deprived him of courage, so that he sinks beneath his burden and is troubled at the very thought of the Almighty, the self-sufficient and eternal Being.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott unfolds the two things in which the Almighty has troubled him, carrying the sense straight into the next verse: that God did not cut him off before the darkness, so that he had never been born, or that, having given him life, he did not hide the darkness from his eyes — a double complaint that Ellicott sets beside Job's earlier cries in ch. 3:11 and 3:20, and which may be understood either of the physical suffering laid on him or of the mental distress and perplexity under which he laboured. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, simply give the plain rendering of the verse, that God has made Job's heart faint and the Almighty has troubled him, letting the bare words carry their own weight.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the softness that Job laments. There is a gracious softness of heart, like Josiah's, whose heart was tender and trembled at the word of God; but this is a grievous softness, in which the Almighty so troubles a man that his heart is unable to bear anything, afraid of everything present as pressing and everything future as threatening. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that Job here lays his collapse honestly at God's door, neither cursing him nor excusing himself, but owning that the strength and courage of his soul have melted under a hand he cannot resist — and that this melting, unlike the melting of repentance, has left him not softened toward God in trust but faint before him in fear, the very posture from which the closing verse will cry out.
17:
The chapter ends in the dark, on a sentence the witnesses render in sharply different ways. As the Authorized Version has it — and as the reformed John Gill, the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry all take it — Job's grief is that he was "not cut off before the darkness," that God did not take him away by death before this dark dispensation came upon him. Gill hears Job amazed, and half wishing, that he had been removed as the righteous are sometimes taken from the evil to come, as Methuselah was before the flood; indeed he reports Aben Ezra's reading of the line as an outright wish, "why was I not cut off?" — or else that Job marvels he was not cut off by the darkness of his afflictions, wondering how he was supported through them. Wesley puts it plainly: God did not cut him off by death before these miseries came, nor cover him by hiding him in the grave.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the peevish side of it, Job quarrelling with God both because he did not die before his troubles, that he might never have seen them, and because he was left to live so long in them, the darkness not covered from his face by burial; yet Henry adds the hope that to the upright there sometimes arises a marvellous light in the darkness. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the verse altogether otherwise, following Mr. Good — "O why can I not draw darkness over my face? why may not thick darkness cover my face?" — and joining it to the verse before: it is not this deep night of affliction, nor the evils he suffers, that have overwhelmed Job, but the fear which the presence of God's majesty inspires. Nothing, Clarke says, so humbles a pious mind as Scriptural apprehensions of the majesty of God; it is easy to contemplate his goodness, but to be brought, conscious of sin, into the presence of his holiness and justice is a thing no human spirit can bear without a Mediator.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, holding the words to the previous verse, takes them of the two respects in which God has troubled him — that he was not cut off before the darkness, or that the darkness was not hidden from his face. So the witnesses close the chapter divided over its last words: whether Job laments that death did not spare him the sight of his sorrows, with Gill, Wesley, and Henry, or confesses that it is not his sorrows at all but the terror of God's majesty that overwhelms him, with Clarke. What none of them doubts is the darkness itself, in which a man who began the chapter longing to find God's seat ends it faint and afraid before the God he has found only as a consuming presence — the lament sinking into shadow, though not, the witnesses would say, into final despair.
